statement: A complete connected [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) of dimension $n \ge 2$ and [constant curvature](c:constant-curvature) $K$ is isometric to a quotient $N/\Gamma$. Here $N$ is the round sphere of radius $1/\sqrt{K}$ if $K > 0$, Euclidean space if $K = 0$, hyperbolic space of curvature $K$ if $K < 0$, and $\Gamma$ is a group of isometries of $N$ acting [freely and properly discontinuously](c:properly-discontinuous-action).

hypotheses.text: The manifold $M$ is [complete](c:geodesic-completeness): every geodesic extends to all times.
The manifold $M$ is connected and has dimension $n \ge 2$.
The sectional curvature of $M$ is the constant $K$.

conclusion: There is a group $\Gamma$ of isometries of the model space $N$, acting freely and properly discontinuously, with $M$ isometric to $N/\Gamma$.

proofs.name: Universal cover and Cartan's theorem
proofs.slogan: Lift to the universal cover, identify the simply connected space with the model by Cartan's theorem, and read the quotient off the deck group.
proofs.scope: The case $n \ge 2$. For $n = 1$ a complete connected curve is a line or a circle, which is a quotient of $\mathbb{R}$.

roles.why: Completeness lifts to the cover and makes the local isometry onto the model a covering map.
Connectedness gives one universal cover and lets the comparison start from a single base point.
Constant curvature fixes the Jacobi fields, so the metric in normal coordinates is the same as the model.

steps.slogan: Pull the metric back to the [universal cover](c:universal-cover) of $M$.
steps.detail: The covering map $p\colon \tilde M \to M$ is a local diffeomorphism, so $\tilde g = p^*g$ is a metric and $p$ is a local isometry. Curvature is local, so $\tilde M$ has curvature $K$. Geodesics of $M$ extend and lift, so $\tilde M$ is complete; the Hopf-Rinow theorem makes geodesic and metric completeness agree.

steps.slogan: Rescale the metric so that $K$ is $1$, $0$ or $-1$.
steps.detail: For $K \neq 0$, replace $\tilde g$ by $|K|\tilde g$. This changes the curvature to $\pm 1$ and keeps completeness. The model $N$ (sphere, Euclidean space or hyperbolic space) is then complete, simply connected and of the same curvature.

steps.slogan: Build a local isometry from $\tilde M$ to the model space by [exponential maps](c:exponential-map).
steps.detail: Fix $p \in \tilde M$, $q \in N$ and a linear isometry $I\colon T_p\tilde M \to T_qN$. Equal constant curvature gives equal Jacobi fields, so $F = \exp_q \circ I \circ \exp_p^{-1}$ preserves the metric on a normal ball. For $K \le 0$, $\exp_p$ is a diffeomorphism and $F$ is global; for $K = 1$ the Cartan-Ambrose-Hicks argument extends $F$ along geodesics from $p$.

steps.slogan: Show that the local isometry is a [covering map](c:covering-space) onto the model, so an isometry.
steps.detail: A local isometry from a complete manifold to a connected manifold is a covering map. The model is simply connected, so this covering has one sheet. Hence $F\colon \tilde M \to N$ is a bijective local isometry, that is an isometry.

steps.slogan: Descend through the [deck group](c:deck-transformation) to write $M$ as a quotient of the model.
steps.detail: The deck group of $p$ acts on $\tilde M$ freely and by isometries of $\tilde g$, and $M = \tilde M/\Gamma'$. Conjugating by $F$ gives a group $\Gamma$ of isometries of $N$, acting freely and [properly discontinuously](c:properly-discontinuous-action), with $M \cong N/\Gamma$.

concepts.c:riemannian-manifold: The manifold carries the metric whose curvature and completeness the proof uses.
concepts.c:constant-curvature: Constant curvature makes the manifold locally the same as the model space.
concepts.c:properly-discontinuous-action: The deck group acts in this way, so the quotient is a manifold.
concepts.c:geodesic-completeness: Completeness lets geodesics lift and makes the local isometry a covering.
concepts.c:universal-cover: The simply connected cover is where the model comparison works.
concepts.c:exponential-map: The exponential maps at the two base points define the comparison map.
concepts.c:covering-space: A local isometry from a complete manifold is a covering, hence a bijection here.
concepts.c:deck-transformation: Deck transformations form the group $\Gamma$ that recovers $M$ from its cover.

source.note: The classical argument of Killing and Hopf through Cartan's theorem on local isometries, as in do Carmo, Riemannian Geometry, and Wolf, Spaces of Constant Curvature.

statement: Let $E$ be a smooth [complex vector bundle](c:complex-vector-bundle) over a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) $X$. A $(0,1)$-[connection](c:connection-on-a-vector-bundle) $\bar\partial_E$ on $E$ with $\bar\partial_E^2 = 0$ is the [Dolbeault operator](c:dolbeault-operator) of a unique structure of [holomorphic vector bundle](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle) on $E$. Conversely, every holomorphic structure gives such an operator.

hypotheses.text: The bundle $E \to X$ is a smooth [complex vector bundle](c:complex-vector-bundle) over a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) $X$.
The operator $\bar\partial_E\colon \Gamma(E) \to \Omega^{0,1}(E)$ is $\mathbb{C}$-linear and satisfies $\bar\partial_E(fs) = \bar\partial f \otimes s + f\,\bar\partial_E s$.
The operator is integrable: $\bar\partial_E^2 = 0$, that is the curvature has no $(0,2)$ part.

conclusion: There is a unique holomorphic structure on $E$ whose local holomorphic sections are exactly the local sections $s$ with $\bar\partial_E s = 0$.

proofs.name: Local frames killed by the operator
proofs.slogan: Solve the integrable gauge equation near each point to get frames killed by the operator, and check that their transition matrices are holomorphic.
proofs.scope: The proof is an outline that rests on the cited analytic existence of local frames (step 3). The converse direction is immediate and is checked in the last step.

roles.why: The smooth bundle gives frames, and the complex manifold gives the holomorphic charts in which transition matrices are tested.
The Leibniz rule makes $\bar\partial_E$ equal to $\bar\partial + A$ in each frame.
The condition $\bar\partial_E^2 = 0$ is the compatibility condition that makes the gauge equation solvable.

steps.slogan: Reduce the holomorphic structure to local frames killed by $\bar\partial_E$.
steps.detail: A holomorphic structure is an atlas of local frames of $E$ whose transition matrices are holomorphic. So it is enough to find, near every point of $X$, a smooth frame $e$ with $\bar\partial_E e = 0$.

steps.slogan: Write the frame condition as an equation $\bar\partial g = -Ag$ for a matrix function.
steps.detail: In a smooth frame, $\bar\partial_E = \bar\partial + A$ for a matrix $A$ of $(0,1)$-forms, by the Leibniz rule. The condition $\bar\partial_E^2 = 0$ reads $\bar\partial A + A \wedge A = 0$. A new frame $e\,g$ is killed by $\bar\partial_E$ exactly when $g$ is invertible and $\bar\partial g = -Ag$.

steps.slogan: Solve the integrable equation near each point by estimates for $\bar\partial$.
steps.detail: Koszul and Malgrange prove that the system $\bar\partial g = -Ag$ with $\bar\partial A + A \wedge A = 0$ has an invertible solution on a small polydisc around each point. They use $\bar\partial$ estimates in the manner of the Newlander-Nirenberg theorem. This is the analytic content that the outline cites.

steps.slogan: Show that the transition matrices of two such frames are [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function).
steps.detail: If $e$ and $e' = e\,h$ are two frames killed by $\bar\partial_E$, then $0 = \bar\partial_E(e\,h) = e\,\bar\partial h$. So $\bar\partial h = 0$ and $h$ is holomorphic and invertible. The frames form a holomorphic atlas.

steps.slogan: Assemble the atlas, and check uniqueness and the converse.
steps.detail: The atlas gives a holomorphic structure whose holomorphic sections are the sections killed by $\bar\partial_E$. Those sections determine the frames, so the structure is unique. Conversely, in a holomorphic frame $\bar\partial_E = \bar\partial$, which has the Leibniz rule and square zero.

concepts.c:complex-vector-bundle: The theorem equips this underlying smooth bundle with a holomorphic structure.
concepts.c:complex-manifold: The base carries the holomorphic charts and the operator $\bar\partial$.
concepts.c:connection-on-a-vector-bundle: The operator is a $(0,1)$-connection, so it equals $\bar\partial + A$ in a frame.
concepts.c:dolbeault-operator: The holomorphic structure is read back as the kernel of this operator.
concepts.c:holomorphic-vector-bundle: This is the structure that the proof constructs on $E$.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphic transition matrices are what make the frame atlas a holomorphic structure.

source.ref: J. L. Koszul and B. Malgrange, Sur certaines structures fibrees complexes, Archiv der Mathematik 9 (1958), 102-109
source.note: The existence of local solutions of the integrable gauge equation (step 3) is the cited analytic input; the other steps are the standard reduction to it.

statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $l$ a prime different from the characteristic of $F$, and suppose that the $l$-cohomological dimension $d$ of $F$ is finite. Then the comparison map from [algebraic K-theory](c:algebraic-k-theory) to étale K-theory, $K_n(F; \mathbb{Z}/l^
u) 	o K^{	ext{ét}}_n(F; \mathbb{Z}/l^
u)$, is an isomorphism for all $n \ge d - 1$ and all $
u \ge 1$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $F$ is a field and $l$ is a prime different from the characteristic of $F$.
The [étale cohomology](c:etale-cohomology) of $F$ with $l$-primary torsion coefficients vanishes above degree $d$, with $d$ finite.

conclusion:
The map $K_n(F; \mathbb{Z}/l^
u) 	o K^{	ext{ét}}_n(F; \mathbb{Z}/l^
u)$ is an isomorphism for every $n \ge d - 1$ and every $
u \ge 1$.

proofs.name: From the norm residue theorem
proofs.slogan: The norm residue isomorphism gives the Beilinson-Lichtenbaum comparison, and a comparison of the two spectral sequences with the cohomological dimension bound gives the K-theory statement.
proofs.scope: The proof is an outline that rests on the cited work. It treats fields with $\mathbb{Z}/l^\nu$ coefficients; the versions for rings of $S$-integers and smooth varieties belong to the same family.

roles.why: The characteristic is prime to $l$, so the roots of unity and étale cohomology with $l$-torsion coefficients are available.
The vanishing of cohomology above degree $d$ fixes the cutoff $n \ge d - 1$ in the comparison.

steps.slogan: Take the norm residue isomorphism from Milnor K-theory to Galois cohomology.
steps.detail: Voevodsky and Rost prove that $K^M_n(F)/l \cong H^n_{\text{ét}}(F, \mu_l^{\otimes n})$ for every field of characteristic different from $l$ and every $n$. This is the Bloch-Kato conjecture. Its proof is the cited work.

steps.slogan: Derive the Beilinson-Lichtenbaum comparison of motivic and étale cohomology.
steps.detail: The Bloch-Kato conjecture implies that $H^s(F, \mathbb{Z}/l(t)) \to H^s_{\text{ét}}(F, \mu_l^{\otimes t})$ is an isomorphism for $s \le t$. Suslin, Voevodsky and Geisser-Levine show this implication.

steps.slogan: Compare the motivic and the étale spectral sequences that converge to K-theory.
steps.detail: The motivic spectral sequence has $E_2$ terms $H^s(F, \mathbb{Z}/l(t))$ and abuts to $K_{2t-s}(F; \mathbb{Z}/l)$. The étale one has étale cohomology as $E_2$ and abuts to étale K-theory. The comparison map is a map of spectral sequences, an isomorphism on the terms with $s \le t$.

steps.slogan: Use the bound $d$ to show that the failing terms only reach low degrees.
steps.detail: A term with $s > t$ vanishes unless $s \le d$, because cohomology vanishes above $d$. Such a term contributes to degree $2t - s \le s - 2 \le d - 2$. So every term in total degree $n \ge d - 1$ lies where the comparison is an isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the abutments agree in all degrees $n \ge d - 1$.
steps.detail:
The map of spectral sequences is an isomorphism on all terms that reach degrees $\ge d - 1$. The convergence of both spectral sequences then gives an isomorphism of $K_n(F; \mathbb{Z}/l^
u)$ and $K^{	ext{ét}}_n(F; \mathbb{Z}/l^
u)$ for $n \ge d - 1$. The case $
u > 1$ follows from $
u = 1$ by induction on the Bockstein sequence.

concepts.c:algebraic-k-theory: The theorem compares this theory with its étale version in high degrees.
concepts.c:etale-cohomology: Étale cohomology is the target of the comparison and vanishes above degree $d$.

source.ref: V. Voevodsky, On motivic cohomology with Z/l-coefficients, Annals of Mathematics 174 (2011), 401-438; the deduction of the Quillen-Lichtenbaum statement is in C. Weibel, The norm residue isomorphism theorem, Journal of Topology 2 (2009), 346-372
source.note: Voevodsky's paper proves the Bloch-Kato conjecture (with Rost's work); the passage to K-theory follows Weibel's survey.

statement: Let $f$ and $g$ be [meromorphic functions](c:meromorphic-function) in [normal form](c:normal-form) at a point $x$ of a nontrivially normed field, for example $\mathbb{C}$. Then $f = g$ on a [punctured neighborhood](c:punctured-neighborhood) of $x$ if and only if $f = g$ on a neighborhood of $x$.

hypotheses.text: The functions map a nontrivially normed field $\mathbb{K}$, such as $\mathbb{C}$, to a normed space.
The function $f$ is meromorphic at $x$ and in [normal form](c:normal-form) there.
The function $g$ is meromorphic at $x$ and in [normal form](c:normal-form) there.

conclusion: The functions agree on a punctured neighborhood of $x$ exactly when they agree on a full neighborhood of $x$.

proofs.name: Compare the orders
proofs.slogan: Equal orders force equal values at the point, by continuity when the order is zero and by the vanishing convention otherwise.
proofs.scope: Both directions. Normal form means that $f$ vanishes near $x$, or $f(z) = (z - x)^n h(z)$ near $x$ with $h$ analytic and $h(x) \neq 0$, where $0^n = 0$ for $n \neq 0$.

roles.why: A nontrivially normed field makes $x$ a limit point of its punctured neighborhoods, so orders and limits at $x$ exist.
Normal form fixes $f(x)$ by the local behavior: the analytic value if the order is $0$, and $0$ otherwise.
Normal form fixes $g(x)$ in the same way, so the two values can be compared.

steps.slogan: Obtain the easy direction by shrinking a neighborhood to a punctured one.
steps.detail: If $f = g$ on a neighborhood $U$ of $x$, then $f = g$ on $U \setminus \{x\}$, which is a punctured neighborhood of $x$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f$ and $g$ have the same meromorphic order at $x$.
steps.detail: The order $\operatorname{ord}_x f$ is the exponent $n$ in $f = (z - x)^n h$ with $h$ analytic and $h(x) \neq 0$, and $\infty$ if $f$ vanishes near $x$. It depends only on $f$ near $x$ off $x$, so $f = g$ there gives $\operatorname{ord}_x f = \operatorname{ord}_x g$.

steps.slogan: In the case of order $0$, show that both functions are continuous at $x$ and agree there.
steps.detail: For a function in normal form, $\operatorname{ord}_x f \ge 0$ exactly when $f$ is [analytic](c:analytic-function) at $x$. With order $0$, both $f$ and $g$ are analytic at $x$, so continuous. Two functions that are continuous at $x$ and agree off $x$ near $x$ agree at $x$ by taking limits.

steps.slogan: In the case of nonzero order, show that both functions vanish at $x$.
steps.detail: For a function in normal form, $\operatorname{ord}_x f = 0$ exactly when $f(x) \neq 0$. At a zero, a pole or a point near which $f$ vanishes, the convention $0^n = 0$ gives $f(x) = 0$. So $f(x) = 0 = g(x)$ when the common order is not $0$.

steps.slogan: Combine the equality at $x$ with the equality on the punctured neighborhood.
steps.detail: In both cases $f(x) = g(x)$. Together with $f = g$ on a punctured neighborhood of $x$, this gives $f = g$ on a full neighborhood of $x$. With the easy direction, the two conditions are equivalent.

concepts.c:meromorphic-function: The order of a meromorphic function at $x$ is the quantity the proof compares.
concepts.c:normal-form: Normal form ties the value at $x$ to the order, which closes the gap at $x$.
concepts.c:punctured-neighborhood: The hypothesis of agreement is only on this set, which omits $x$ itself.
concepts.c:analytic-function: Order $0$ in normal form means analytic, hence continuous at $x$.

source.note: mathlib compares orders with meromorphicOrderAt_congr, then splits on order 0 (meromorphicOrderAt_nonneg_iff_analyticAt, ContinuousAt.eventuallyEq_nhds_iff_eventuallyEq_nhdsNE) and on nonzero order (meromorphicOrderAt_eq_zero_iff, eventuallyEq_nhds_of_eventuallyEq_nhdsNE).

statement: Let $X$ be a set of [lattices](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) of [covolume](c:covolume) $1$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, with the topology of $SL_n(\mathbb{R})/SL_n(\mathbb{Z})$. Then $X$ is [relatively compact](c:relatively-compact-subspace) if and only if some $\varepsilon > 0$ satisfies $\|v\| \ge \varepsilon$ for every nonzero vector $v$ of every lattice in $X$.

hypotheses.text: Every lattice of $X$ has [covolume](c:covolume) $1$.
The space of such lattices has the quotient topology of $SL_n(\mathbb{R})/SL_n(\mathbb{Z})$, where $g$ stands for the lattice $g\mathbb{Z}^n$.

conclusion: The set $X$ has compact closure exactly when the lengths of nonzero lattice vectors in $X$ have a positive lower bound.

proofs.name: Successive minima and converging bases
proofs.slogan: Bound the successive minima by Minkowski's second theorem, extract converging short vectors, and rebuild each lattice from them.
proofs.scope: Both directions, for $n \ge 1$. The space of lattices is metrizable, so relative compactness is tested on sequences.

roles.why: Covolume $1$ bounds the product of the minima, makes indices integers, and keeps the limit unimodular.
The quotient topology makes the shortest vector length continuous and defines convergence by converging bases.

steps.slogan: Show that the shortest vector length is continuous and positive on the space of lattices.
steps.detail: Put $\lambda_1(g\mathbb{Z}^n) = \min_{m \neq 0} \|gm\|$, which is positive because a lattice is discrete. If $\|g' - g\|\,\|g^{-1}\| < \delta$, then $\|g'm\|/\|gm\| \in (1 - \delta, 1 + \delta)$ for all $m \neq 0$, so $\lambda_1$ is continuous. On the compact closure of a relatively compact $X$ it has a positive minimum $\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Bound all [successive minima](c:successive-minima) of the lattices in $X$.
steps.detail: Minkowski's second theorem gives $\lambda_1 \cdots \lambda_n \le 2^n/\operatorname{vol}(B^n)$ for covolume $1$. With $\lambda_1 \ge \varepsilon$ and $\lambda_1 \le \cdots \le \lambda_n$, this gives $\lambda_n \le C = 2^n/(\operatorname{vol}(B^n)\,\varepsilon^{n-1})$. So each lattice of $X$ has $n$ independent vectors of norm at most $C$.

steps.slogan: Extract converging short vectors from a sequence and show that their spans have constant index.
steps.detail: Take $\Lambda_k \in X$ with independent $v^{(k)}_i \in \Lambda_k$ of norm at most $C$. A subsequence has $v^{(k)}_i \to v_i$. The index $[\Lambda_k : L_k] = |\det V_k|$ is a positive integer, at most $C^n$ by Hadamard's inequality, so it is a constant $m$ on a subsequence. Then $|\det V| = m$ for the limit matrix $V$.

steps.slogan: Describe each lattice as a fixed overlattice of the span of its short vectors.
steps.detail: Since $m\Lambda_k \subseteq L_k$, the lattice $\Lambda_k$ equals $V_k H_k$ for a group $H_k$ with $\mathbb{Z}^n \subseteq H_k \subseteq \tfrac1m \mathbb{Z}^n$. There are finitely many such groups, so $H_k = H$ on a subsequence.

steps.slogan: Show that the lattices $V_k H$ converge to the lattice $VH$ of covolume $1$.
steps.detail: Let $B$ be a basis matrix of $H$. Then $V_k B \to VB$, so $\Lambda_k \to VB\mathbb{Z}^n$ in the quotient topology. By continuity of the [determinant](c:determinant) the limit has covolume $1$. So every sequence in $X$ has a convergent subsequence in the space of lattices.

steps.slogan: Combine both directions into the equivalence of the theorem.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives the bound $\varepsilon$ for a relatively compact $X$. Steps 2 to 5 give a convergent subsequence of any sequence in $X$ when the bound holds. The space is metrizable, so $X$ is then relatively compact.

concepts.c:lattice-discrete-subgroup: The objects of the theorem are these discrete subgroups, rebuilt from short basis-like vectors.
concepts.c:covolume: Covolume $1$ bounds the minima and makes the index an integer.
concepts.c:relatively-compact-subspace: The theorem characterizes this property by a lower bound on vector lengths.
concepts.c:successive-minima: Bounded successive minima give independent short vectors in every lattice.
concepts.c:determinant: The determinant measures the index of the span and the covolume of the limit.

source.note: The classical proof of Mahler's selection theorem, as in Cassels, An Introduction to the Geometry of Numbers, Chapter V, with Minkowski's second theorem from Chapter VIII.

statement: Let $A$ be an [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety) over a number field $F$ with ordinary [good reduction](c:has-good-reduction) at every prime above $p$, and let $F_\infty/F$ be the cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension with layers $F_n$. Then the restriction maps $\mathrm{Sel}_{p^\infty}(A/F_n) \to \mathrm{Sel}_{p^\infty}(A/F_\infty)^{\mathrm{Gal}(F_\infty/F_n)}$ of [Selmer groups](c:selmer-group) have finite kernel and cokernel, of orders bounded independently of $n$.

hypotheses.text: The variety $A$ is an [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety) over a number field $F$.
The variety $A$ has ordinary [good reduction](c:has-good-reduction) at every prime of $F$ above $p$.
The field $F_\infty$ is the cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension of $F$, and $F_n$ is its layer of degree $p^n$ over $F$.

conclusion: For every $n \ge 0$ the kernel and cokernel of the restriction map are finite, and their orders have a bound that does not depend on $n$.

proofs.name: Snake lemma on the Selmer diagram
proofs.slogan: Compare the Selmer sequences of the layer and of the limit, apply the snake lemma, and bound the global and local kernels independently of the layer.
proofs.scope: The proof is an outline that rests on the cited work for the local estimates at primes above $p$. The Selmer groups are the $p$-primary ones, defined by the usual local conditions.

roles.why: The torsion $A[p^\infty]$ and its Galois cohomology define the Selmer groups that the diagram compares.
Ordinary good reduction gives finite torsion in the tower and the formal group sequence that bounds the local kernels at $p$.
The group $\mathbb{Z}_p$ has cohomological dimension $1$, and the extension is totally ramified above $p$ and has finitely many primes over each other prime.

steps.slogan: Place the restriction maps in a commutative diagram with exact Selmer rows.
steps.detail: Write $\Gamma_n = \mathrm{Gal}(F_\infty/F_n)$. The $F_n$ row is $0 \to \mathrm{Sel}(F_n) \to H^1(F_n, A[p^\infty]) \to \prod_v H^1(F_{n,v}, A)[p^\infty]$. The second row has the $\Gamma_n$-invariants of the same sequence over $F_\infty$. The vertical restriction maps are $s$, $h$ and $g$.

steps.slogan: Control the global middle map by inflation-restriction and the dimension of $\mathbb{Z}_p$.
steps.detail: The kernel of $h$ is $H^1(\Gamma_n, A(F_\infty)[p^\infty])$, and its cokernel lies in $H^2(\Gamma_n, \cdot) = 0$ because $\Gamma_n \cong \mathbb{Z}_p$ has dimension $1$. Ordinary reduction makes $A(F_\infty)[p^\infty]$ finite, so $\ker h$ is finite of order at most $|A(F_\infty)[p^\infty]|$, for every $n$.

steps.slogan: Apply the snake lemma to bound the Selmer kernel and cokernel by the local kernels.
steps.detail: The snake lemma on the two rows gives an exact sequence $0 \to \ker s \to \ker h \to \ker g \to \operatorname{coker} s \to \operatorname{coker} h = 0$. So $|\ker s| \le |\ker h|$ and $|\operatorname{coker} s| \le |\ker g|$.

steps.slogan: Bound the local kernels at the primes not above $p$.
steps.detail: For a prime $v \nmid p$ the extension is unramified, so the decomposition groups are procyclic and $\ker g_v$ is a finite cohomology group. Its order is bounded by the $p$-part of the Tamagawa number of $A$ at $v$, and $v$ has finitely many primes above it in $F_\infty$. So this contribution is bounded independently of $n$.

steps.slogan: Bound the local kernels at the primes above $p$ using ordinary reduction.
steps.detail: At $w \mid p$ the extension is totally ramified. Ordinary reduction gives a sequence from the formal group of $A$ to the reduced group over the residue field. Mazur shows that $\ker g_w$ is bounded by the $p$-part of the finite reduced group, independently of $n$.

steps.slogan: Combine the global and local bounds into a bound independent of $n$.
steps.detail: By the snake lemma, $|\ker s| \le |\ker h|$ and $|\operatorname{coker} s| \le |\ker g|$, and $\ker g$ is the product of the finitely many local kernels. Each factor is finite and bounded independently of $n$ by the two local steps. So $\ker s$ and $\operatorname{coker} s$ are finite with orders bounded independently of $n$.

concepts.c:abelian-variety: The torsion points of the variety give the Galois modules behind the Selmer groups.
concepts.c:has-good-reduction: Ordinary good reduction at $p$ is what bounds the local kernels above $p$.
concepts.c:selmer-group: The theorem compares the Selmer groups of the layers with that of the limit.

source.ref: B. Mazur, Rational points of abelian varieties with values in towers of number fields, Inventiones Mathematicae 18 (1972), 183-266
source.note: R. Greenberg, Iwasawa theory for elliptic curves (Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1716, 1999) gives the elliptic curve case in the form outlined here.

statement: Let $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ be points on the lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ of a [triangle](c:triangle) $ABC$, different from the vertices. Then the three [circles](c:circle) $AB'C'$, $BC'A'$ and $CA'B'$ have a common point.

hypotheses.text: The points $A$, $B$, $C$ form a nondegenerate [triangle](c:triangle).
The points $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ lie on the lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ and differ from the vertices.

conclusion: The circles $AB'C'$, $BC'A'$ and $CA'B'$ pass through one common point $M$.

proofs.name: Directed angle chase
proofs.slogan: Take the second common point of two circles and add directed angles at that point to show that it lies on the third circle.
proofs.scope: Directed angles between lines, modulo $\pi$, cover every configuration. If the first two circles are tangent at $C'$, then $M = C'$ and the line $MC'$ is the common tangent.

roles.why: The three side lines of the triangle give the angle sum $\angle(AC, AB) + \angle(AB, BC) = \angle(AC, BC)$.
The points on the side lines define the three circles and put the chords $MB'$, $MC'$, $MA'$ at the vertices.

steps.slogan: Let $M$ be the second common point of the circles $AB'C'$ and $BC'A'$.
steps.detail: Both circles pass through $C'$. Let $M$ be their other common point, or $M = C'$ if they are tangent at $C'$.

steps.slogan: Move the angle at $M$ onto the vertex $A$ using the circle $AB'C'$.
steps.detail: The points $A$, $B'$, $C'$, $M$ lie on one circle and form a [cyclic quadrilateral](c:cyclic-quadrilateral). So $\angle(MB', MC') = \angle(AB', AC') = \angle(AC, AB)$, because $B'$ is on $AC$ and $C'$ is on $AB$.

steps.slogan: Move the angle at $M$ onto the vertex $B$ using the circle $BC'A'$.
steps.detail: In the same way $B$, $C'$, $A'$, $M$ are concyclic, so $\angle(MC', MA') = \angle(BC', BA') = \angle(AB, BC)$.

steps.slogan: Add the two angles at $M$ to find the angle $\angle(MB', MA')$.
steps.detail: Directed angles add, so $\angle(MB', MA') = \angle(AC, AB) + \angle(AB, BC) = \angle(AC, BC)$. This equals $\angle(CB', CA')$, because $CB'$ is the line $AC$ and $CA'$ is the line $BC$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $M$, $C$, $A'$, $B'$ lie on one circle.
steps.detail: The equality $\angle(MB', MA') = \angle(CB', CA')$ is the criterion for the four points to be concyclic. So $M$ lies on the circle $CA'B'$, and on the other two circles by construction.

concepts.c:triangle: The three side lines of the triangle carry all the angles that are added.
concepts.c:circle: The three circles are the objects whose common point is found.
concepts.c:cyclic-quadrilateral: Concyclic points give equal directed angles on the same chord.

source.note: The classical angle chase for Miquel's theorem, as in Coxeter and Greitzer, Geometry Revisited, with directed angles to cover all configurations.

statement: Let $M$ be a framed $n$-[manifold](c:manifold) and $X$ a pointed $(n-1)$-connected space. Then the natural map from the [factorization homology](c:factorization-homology) $\int_M \Omega^n X$ of the [$E_n$-algebra](c:e-n-algebra) $\Omega^n X$ (the $n$-fold [loop space](c:loop-space)) to the space of [compactly supported maps](c:compactly-supported-mapping-space) $\mathrm{Map}_c(M, X)$ is an equivalence.

hypotheses.text: The space $M$ is a framed smooth $n$-[manifold](c:manifold), with $n \ge 1$.
The pointed space $X$ is $(n-1)$-connected: its homotopy groups vanish up to degree $n - 1$.

conclusion: The natural map $\int_M \Omega^n X \to \mathrm{Map}_c(M, X)$ is an equivalence of spaces.

proofs.name: Excision and induction over handles
proofs.slogan: Compare the two sides on discs and show that both satisfy excision, then build the manifold from discs by induction.
proofs.scope: The proof is an outline that rests on the cited work for the excision of compactly supported maps. The unframed case replaces $\Omega^n X$ by the factorization algebra $U \mapsto \mathrm{Map}_c(U, X)$, and the equivariant version is another member of the family.

roles.why: The framing lets the $E_n$-algebra define factorization homology on $M$, and a handle decomposition builds $M$ from discs.
The connectivity of $X$ is what makes compactly supported maps satisfy excision.

steps.slogan: Give $\Omega^n X$ its $E_n$-structure and $U \mapsto \mathrm{Map}_c(U, X)$ its factorization structure.
steps.detail: Pointed maps $S^n \to X$ form $\Omega^n X$, an [$E_n$-algebra](c:e-n-algebra) by composing little cubes. For open $U \subseteq M$, $\mathrm{Map}_c(U, X)$ is covariant in $U$ (extend by the base point), and it sends disjoint unions to products.

steps.slogan: Define the comparison map by the universal property of factorization homology.
steps.detail: The assignment $U \mapsto \mathrm{Map}_c(U, X)$ is a locally constant factorization algebra with value $\Omega^n X$ on a disc. [Factorization homology](c:factorization-homology) is the universal such object built from the algebra on discs. This gives the natural map $\int_M \Omega^n X \to \mathrm{Map}_c(M, X)$.

steps.slogan: Check that the comparison map is an equivalence on a disc.
steps.detail: $\mathrm{Map}_c(\mathbb{R}^n, X)$ is the space of pointed maps $S^n \to X$, which is $\Omega^n X$. The factorization homology of a disc is the algebra itself. So the map is the identity of $\Omega^n X$.

steps.slogan: Show that compactly supported maps satisfy [excision](c:excision) when $X$ is $(n-1)$-connected.
steps.detail: For a collar-gluing $M = M_0 \cup_{N \times \mathbb{R}} M_1$, factorization homology is the relative tensor product of the pieces. Lurie shows that $\mathrm{Map}_c(-, X)$ has the same gluing property, and the connectivity of $X$ is exactly what this comparison needs.

steps.slogan: Build $M$ from discs by a [handle decomposition](c:handle-decomposition) and conclude by induction.
steps.detail: Both sides satisfy excision and agree on discs and finite disjoint unions of discs. A manifold with finite handle decomposition is glued from discs, so the map is an equivalence for it. A general $M$ is an increasing union of such pieces, and both sides commute with these unions.

concepts.c:manifold: The manifold is cut into discs and handles for the induction.
concepts.c:factorization-homology: Factorization homology is the left side of the equivalence.
concepts.c:e-n-algebra: The $n$-fold loop space has this structure, which factorization homology uses.
concepts.c:loop-space: The coefficient algebra is the $n$-fold loop space of $X$.
concepts.c:compactly-supported-mapping-space: This mapping space is the right side of the equivalence.
concepts.c:excision: Excision lets the equivalence pass from pieces to the glued manifold.
concepts.c:handle-decomposition: Handles are the pieces by which the induction builds the manifold.

source.ref: J. Lurie, Higher Algebra, 2017, Theorem 5.5.6.6 (nonabelian Poincare duality)
source.note: Earlier forms are due to Segal and Salvatore for configuration spaces; the excision step is the part of Lurie's argument that uses the connectivity of $X$.

statement: Two two-sided [Bernoulli schemes](c:bernoulli-scheme) on finite alphabets that have the same [Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy](c:kolmogorov-sinai-entropy) are isomorphic as [measure-preserving systems](c:measure-preserving-system): a bimeasurable measure-preserving bijection, defined off a null set, conjugates the two shifts.

hypotheses.text: The systems are two-sided shifts on finite alphabets with product measures $p^{\mathbb{Z}}$ and $q^{\mathbb{Z}}$, that is [Bernoulli schemes](c:bernoulli-scheme).
The two shifts have the same [entropy](c:kolmogorov-sinai-entropy): $-\sum_i p_i \log p_i = -\sum_j q_j \log q_j$.

conclusion: There is a measure-preserving isomorphism between the two systems that carries one shift to the other.

proofs.name: Finitely determined processes
proofs.slogan: Show that Bernoulli processes are finitely determined, copy one inside the other, and correct the copies into a convergent sequence of generating partitions.
proofs.scope: The proof is an outline that rests on the cited work. It covers finite alphabets; countable alphabets and infinite entropy belong to the same family.

roles.why: Independence of coordinates makes each shift finitely determined and gives the generating partitions that are copied.
Equal entropy gives room to copy one process inside the other and makes the limit partition generate.

steps.slogan: Compute the entropy of a Bernoulli shift and recall that entropy is an isomorphism invariant.
steps.detail: Kolmogorov and Sinai show that the entropy of a system is the same for isomorphic systems and equals $-\sum_i p_i \log p_i$ for the Bernoulli shift of $p$. Equal entropy is therefore necessary, and Ornstein proves that it is sufficient.

steps.slogan: Define the $\bar d$ distance between processes and the finitely determined property.
steps.detail: The $\bar d$ distance of two stationary processes is the least expected fraction of coordinates in which a joining of the two differs. A process is finitely determined if every process with nearby finite-dimensional distributions and nearby entropy is $\bar d$-close to it.

steps.slogan: Show that every Bernoulli process is finitely determined.
steps.detail: Ornstein proves that the independent process $p^{\mathbb{Z}}$ is finitely determined. The argument compares the typical blocks of a nearby process with those of the independent process through a counting estimate.

steps.slogan: Copy a Bernoulli process inside a system of the same entropy.
steps.detail: Let $T$ be the shift of $p$ with generator $P$, and $S$ the shift of $q$. Sinai's factor theorem and Ornstein's copying lemma give, for each $\varepsilon$, a finite [partition](c:finpartition) $Q$ of the space of $S$ whose process is $\bar d$-within $\varepsilon$ of $(T, P)$.

steps.slogan: Correct the copies step by step into a Cauchy sequence of partitions.
steps.detail: The finitely determined property keeps each corrected copy close to $(T, P)$, which lets Ornstein replace $Q_k$ by a slightly changed $Q_{k+1}$ that also captures more of a fixed generator of $S$. The sizes of the changes are summable, so the partitions $Q_k$ converge.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit of the corrected partitions to get the isomorphism.
steps.detail: The limit partition has exactly the distribution of $P$, so its shift process is independent with weights $p$. It generates the whole $\sigma$-algebra of $S$, so it defines a measure-preserving isomorphism from $S$ to $T$.

concepts.c:bernoulli-scheme: These independent shifts are the systems that the proof compares and copies.
concepts.c:kolmogorov-sinai-entropy: Entropy is the invariant whose equality the proof turns into an isomorphism.
concepts.c:measure-preserving-system: The isomorphism must preserve the measure and commute with the shifts.
concepts.c:finpartition: Finite partitions carry the processes that are copied and corrected.

source.ref: D. S. Ornstein, Bernoulli shifts with the same entropy are isomorphic, Advances in Mathematics 4 (1970), 337-352
source.note: A textbook account is P. C. Shields, The Theory of Bernoulli Shifts, University of Chicago Press, 1973.

statement: Let $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ be points on the lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ of a [triangle](c:triangle) $ABC$, different from the vertices. Then the circles $AB'C'$, $BC'A'$, $CA'B'$ pass through a common point $P$, the pivot. The lines $PA'$, $PB'$, $PC'$ make the same directed angle with $BC$, $CA$, $AB$.

hypotheses.text: The points $A$, $B$, $C$ form a nondegenerate [triangle](c:triangle).
The points $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ lie on the lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ and differ from the vertices.

conclusion: The three circles have a common point $P$, and $\angle(PA', BC) = \angle(PB', CA) = \angle(PC', AB)$ as directed angles.

proofs.name: Equal angles at the pivot
proofs.slogan: Show that the second intersection of two circles sees the three side lines at one angle, and that this equal angle puts it on the third circle.
proofs.scope: Directed angles between lines, modulo $\pi$. If the first two circles are tangent at $C'$, then $P = C'$ and the line $PC'$ is the common tangent.

roles.why: The triangle supplies the side lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ against which the angles at $P$ are measured.
The points on the sides define the three circles and the chords $PA'$, $PB'$, $PC'$.

steps.slogan: Let $P$ be the second common point of the circles $AB'C'$ and $BC'A'$.
steps.detail: Both circles pass through $C'$. Let $P$ be their other common point, or $P = C'$ if they are tangent at $C'$.

steps.slogan: Read the angles at $A'$ and $C'$ on the chord $PB$ of the circle $BC'A'$.
steps.detail: The points $B$, $C'$, $A'$, $P$ are concyclic, so $\angle(A'P, A'B) = \angle(C'P, C'B)$. The line $A'B$ is $BC$ and the line $C'B$ is $AB$. Hence $\angle(PA', BC) = \angle(PC', AB)$.

steps.slogan: Read the angles at $B'$ and $C'$ on the chord $PA$ of the circle $AB'C'$.
steps.detail: The points $A$, $B'$, $C'$, $P$ are concyclic, so $\angle(B'P, B'A) = \angle(C'P, C'A)$. The line $B'A$ is $CA$ and the line $C'A$ is $AB$. Hence $\angle(PB', CA) = \angle(PC', AB)$.

steps.slogan: Chain the two equalities to get one angle $\theta$ at all three side lines.
steps.detail: Set $\theta = \angle(PC', AB)$. The two previous steps give $\angle(PA', BC) = \theta = \angle(PB', CA)$. This is the equal-angle part of the conclusion.

steps.slogan: Show that $P$ lies on the circle $CA'B'$ because the chord $PC$ subtends the same angle at $A'$ and $B'$.
steps.detail: The lines $A'C$ and $B'C$ are $BC$ and $CA$, so $\angle(A'P, A'C) = \theta = \angle(B'P, B'C)$. Equal directed angles on the chord $PC$ from $A'$ and $B'$ make $P$, $C$, $A'$, $B'$ concyclic. So $P$ is on all three circles.

concepts.c:triangle: The side lines of the triangle are the lines against which the equal angle is measured.

source.note: The pivot form of Miquel's theorem, proved by the equal-angle argument, as in Coxeter and Greitzer, Geometry Revisited.

statement: For every [first-order](c:first-order-logic) formula $\varphi(x_1, \dots, x_k)$ of set theory, [ZF](c:zf-set-theory) proves that every [ordinal](c:ordinal) $\alpha$ lies below a limit ordinal $\beta$ such that $\varphi$ is absolute for $V_\beta$: for all $x_1, \dots, x_k \in V_\beta$, $\varphi^{V_\beta}(x_1, \dots, x_k) \leftrightarrow \varphi(x_1, \dots, x_k)$.

hypotheses.text: The expression $\varphi(x_1, \dots, x_k)$ is a [first-order](c:first-order-logic) formula in the language $\{\in\}$.
The number $\alpha$ is an [ordinal](c:ordinal).
The background theory is [ZF](c:zf-set-theory); the axiom of replacement is used and choice is not.

conclusion: There is a limit ordinal $\beta > \alpha$ such that $\varphi^{V_\beta}(\vec x) \leftrightarrow \varphi(\vec x)$ for all $\vec x \in V_\beta$.

proofs.name: Close a level under witnesses
proofs.slogan: Close a level of the hierarchy under witnesses of the existential subformulas, then show by induction on the formula that the level reflects each subformula.
proofs.scope: One formula at a time: the theorem is a schema, and ZF proves each instance. Other reflection principles, such as the proof-theoretic and large cardinal forms, are further members of the family.

roles.why: A formula has finitely many existential subformulas, so finitely many witness functions need closure.
The ordinal $\alpha$ is the start of the chain that builds $\beta$ above it.
Replacement makes the witness bounds exist, and the [cumulative hierarchy](c:cumulative-hierarchy) exhausts the universe.

steps.slogan: List the existential subformulas of $\varphi$ after rewriting with $\neg$, $\wedge$ and $\exists$.
steps.detail: Rewrite $\varphi$ with only $\neg$, $\wedge$ and $\exists$. Let $\psi_1, \dots, \psi_m$ be the subformulas of the form $\exists y\, \chi(\vec x, y)$. Only these need witnesses.

steps.slogan: Bound the rank of a least witness for each existential subformula.
steps.detail: For an ordinal $\gamma$ let $g_i(\gamma)$ be the least $\delta > \gamma$ such that every tuple $\vec x \in V_\gamma$ with $\psi_i(\vec x)$ has a witness in $V_\delta$. The [axiom of replacement](c:axiom-of-replacement) makes $g_i$ a well-defined class function, since $V_\gamma^k$ is a set and ranks of witnesses are bounded by a supremum.

steps.slogan: Build $\beta$ as the supremum of an $\omega$-chain closed under all witness bounds.
steps.detail: Put $\gamma_0 = \alpha + 1$, $\gamma_{j+1} = \max(\gamma_j + 1, g_1(\gamma_j), \dots, g_m(\gamma_j))$ and $\beta = \sup_j \gamma_j$. Then $\beta > \alpha$ is a limit ordinal and $V_\beta = \bigcup_j V_{\gamma_j}$. A tuple in $V_\beta$ lies in some $V_{\gamma_j}$, so its witness lies in $V_{\gamma_{j+1}} \subseteq V_\beta$.

steps.slogan: Prove by induction on subformulas that $V_\beta$ and $V$ agree on every subformula of $\varphi$.
steps.detail: Atomic formulas agree because $V_\beta$ is transitive. Negation and conjunction commute with relativization. For $\exists y\, \chi$, a witness in $V_\beta$ is a witness in $V$. Conversely a witness in $V$ exists in $V_\beta$ by step 3, and $\chi$ agrees there by the induction hypothesis.

concepts.c:first-order-logic: The proof is an induction on the structure of a first-order formula.
concepts.c:ordinal: The levels $V_\gamma$ are indexed by ordinals, and $\beta$ is a limit ordinal.
concepts.c:zf-set-theory: The theory supplies the axioms, above all replacement, that the proof needs.
concepts.c:cumulative-hierarchy: The levels $V_\beta$ are the structures that reflect the universe.
concepts.c:axiom-of-replacement: Replacement turns the choice of witness ranks into a class function.

source.note: The Levy-Montague argument, as in Jech, Set Theory (3rd ed., 2003), chapter 12, and Kunen, Set Theory (1980), chapter IV.

statement: For an integer $n \ge 1$ let $a_n = n!/\big(\sqrt{2n}\,(n/e)^n\big)$ be the Stirling sequence, with [factorial](c:factorial) $n!$. Then $\log a_n - \log a_{n+1} \le \dfrac{1}{12\,n\,(n+1)}$, where $\log$ is the natural [logarithm](c:logarithm).

hypotheses.text: The index $n$ is an integer with $n \ge 1$.

conclusion: The decrease $\log a_n - \log a_{n+1}$ of the Stirling sequence at step $n$ is at most $\frac{1}{12\,n\,(n+1)}$.

formal.difference: The declaration holds for every natural $n$, including $0$, where Lean reads $1/0$ as $0$ and stirlingSeq 0 as $0$. For $n \ge 1$ it states the same inequality.

proofs.name: Series in the square of one over $2n+1$
proofs.slogan: Write the step as a power series in $x^2$ with $x = 1/(2n+1)$, bound each coefficient by one third, and sum the geometric series.
proofs.scope: All integers $n \ge 1$. The series is exact, so the same steps show that the decrease is positive.

roles.why: A positive index keeps $x = 1/(2n+1)$ in $(0, 1)$, so the series and the geometric sum converge.

steps.slogan: Compute the step $\log a_n - \log a_{n+1}$ in closed form.
steps.detail: Since $a_n = n!\,e^n/(\sqrt{2}\,n^{n+1/2})$ and $(n+1)! = (n+1)\,n!$, the ratio is $a_n/a_{n+1} = \big((n+1)/n\big)^{n+1/2}/e$. So $\log a_n - \log a_{n+1} = (n + \tfrac12)\log\tfrac{n+1}{n} - 1$.

steps.slogan: Expand the [logarithm](c:logarithm) as a power series in $x = 1/(2n+1)$.
steps.detail: With $x = \frac{1}{2n+1}$ we have $\frac{n+1}{n} = \frac{1+x}{1-x}$ and $n + \frac12 = \frac{1}{2x}$. The [Mercator series](c:mercator-series) for $\log(1 \pm x)$ gives $\log\frac{1+x}{1-x} = 2\sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{x^{2k+1}}{2k+1}$. So $\log a_n - \log a_{n+1} = \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{x^{2k}}{2k+1}$.

steps.slogan: Bound each coefficient $1/(2k+1)$ by $1/3$ for $k \ge 1$.
steps.detail: All terms are positive and $2k + 1 \ge 3$ for $k \ge 1$. So $\sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{x^{2k}}{2k+1} \le \frac13 \sum_{k \ge 1} x^{2k}$.

steps.slogan: Sum the [geometric series](c:geometric-series) in $x^2$.
steps.detail: Since $0 < x^2 < 1$, the sum is $\sum_{k \ge 1} x^{2k} = \frac{x^2}{1 - x^2}$. So the bound is $\frac{x^2}{3(1 - x^2)}$.

steps.slogan: Simplify the bound to $\frac{1}{12\,n\,(n+1)}$.

concepts.c:factorial: The Stirling sequence is built from the factorial, whose ratio gives the step.
concepts.c:logarithm: The step is a logarithm of a ratio, expanded as a power series.
concepts.c:mercator-series: This series expands the logarithm of $(1+x)/(1-x)$.
concepts.c:geometric-series: The bounded series is a geometric series in $x^2$ with a closed sum.

source.note: mathlib expands the step as a series (log_stirlingSeq_sdiff_hasSum), compares it termwise with the series of r^(j+1)/3 (hasSum_le), and sums that with hasSum_geometric_of_lt_one.

statement: Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be [consistent](c:consistent-theory) [first-order theories](c:first-order-theory) in languages $L_1$ and $L_2$, and let $L = L_1 \cap L_2$. If some complete $L$-theory $T_0$ is provable in both $T_1$ and $T_2$, then $T_1 \cup T_2$ is consistent.

hypotheses.text: The theories $T_1$ and $T_2$ are [consistent](c:consistent-theory) first-order theories in the languages $L_1$ and $L_2$.
A complete $L$-theory $T_0$ is provable from $T_1$ and from $T_2$, where $L = L_1 \cap L_2$.

conclusion: The theory $T_1 \cup T_2$ in the language $L_1 \cup L_2$ is consistent.

proofs.name: From Craig interpolation
proofs.slogan: Assume the union is inconsistent, reduce to two sentences by compactness, interpolate in the common language, and contradict the completeness of the shared theory.
proofs.scope: First-order logic with equality. The proof takes the Craig interpolation theorem as known.

roles.why: Each case of the last step makes $T_1$ or $T_2$ inconsistent.
Completeness puts the interpolant or its negation into $T_0$, hence into both theories.

steps.slogan: Suppose that $T_1 \cup T_2$ is inconsistent and reduce to two sentences.
steps.detail: By the compactness theorem a finite part of $T_1 \cup T_2$ is inconsistent. Let $\sigma_1$ be the conjunction of the axioms taken from $T_1$ and $\sigma_2$ the conjunction of those from $T_2$. Then $\sigma_1 \wedge \sigma_2$ is inconsistent, so $\sigma_1 \models \neg\sigma_2$.

steps.slogan: Find a sentence $\theta$ of the common language $L$ between $\sigma_1$ and $\neg\sigma_2$.
steps.detail:
Craig interpolation applied to the valid implication $\sigma_1 	o 
eg\sigma_2$ gives an $L$-[sentence](c:first-order-sentence) $	heta$ with $\sigma_1 \models 	heta$ and $	heta \models 
eg\sigma_2$. So $T_1 \vdash 	heta$ and $T_2 \vdash 
eg	heta$.

steps.slogan: Use the completeness of $T_0$ to derive a contradiction in each case.
steps.detail:
Since $T_0$ is complete, $T_0 \vdash 	heta$ or $T_0 \vdash 
eg	heta$. In the first case $T_2 \vdash 	heta$, and $T_2 \vdash 
eg	heta$, so $T_2$ is inconsistent. In the second case $T_1 \vdash 
eg	heta$ and $T_1 \vdash 	heta$, so $T_1$ is inconsistent. Both cases contradict the hypothesis, so $T_1 \cup T_2$ is consistent.

concepts.c:consistent-theory: The contradiction in each case is with the consistency of $T_1$ or $T_2$.
concepts.c:first-order-theory: The theories are sets of first-order sentences, to which compactness and interpolation apply.
concepts.c:first-order-sentence: The interpolant is a sentence in the common language.

source.note: The standard derivation of Robinson's joint consistency theorem from Craig interpolation (the two theorems are equivalent), as in Chang and Keisler, Model Theory.

proofs.name: Alternating elementary chains
proofs.slogan: Alternate elementary extensions of a model of the first theory and a model of the second, and merge the unions of the two chains along the common language.
proofs.scope: First-order theories with equality in arbitrary languages. The proof is model-theoretic and needs no interpolation theorem.

roles.why: A consistent theory has a model, which starts each chain.
Completeness of $T_0$ makes the $L$-reducts elementarily equivalent, which every amalgamation step needs.

steps.slogan: Choose models $A_0 \models T_1$ and $B_0 \models T_2$ and compare their $L$-reducts.
steps.detail: A [consistent](c:consistent-theory) theory has a model by the completeness theorem. Both $A_0$ and $B_0$ satisfy the complete theory $T_0$, so their $L$-reducts are [elementarily equivalent](c:elementary-equivalence).

steps.slogan: Extend $A_0$ elementarily so that the $L$-reduct of $B_0$ embeds elementarily into it.
steps.detail: Take the $L_1$-[diagram](c:diagram-of-a-first-order-structure) of $A_0$ with the $L$-elementary diagram of $B_0$, using new constants for elements of $B_0$. A finite part is satisfiable: its $L$-part says $\exists \bar y\, \chi(\bar y)$, true in $B_0$ and so in $A_0$, which gives witnesses. By compactness there is an $L_1$-elementary extension $A_1$ of $A_0$ with an $L$-[elementary embedding](c:elementary-embedding) of $B_0 \restriction L$ into $A_1 \restriction L$.

steps.slogan: Alternate the construction to build two interleaved chains of models.
steps.detail: Exchange the roles of $L_1$ and $L_2$ to extend $B_0$ to $B_1$, with an $L$-elementary embedding $A_1 \restriction L \to B_1 \restriction L$, and repeat forever. The result is $L_1$-elementary chain $A_0 \preceq A_1 \preceq \cdots$ and $L_2$-elementary chain $B_0 \preceq B_1 \preceq \cdots$, with $L$-elementary maps $A_k \to B_k \to A_{k+1}$ that compose to the inclusion.

steps.slogan: Take the unions of the two chains and show that their $L$-reducts are isomorphic.
steps.detail: By Tarski's elementary chain theorem, $A_\omega = \bigcup_k A_k$ is an elementary extension of $A_0$ in $L_1$ and $B_\omega = \bigcup_k B_k$ one of $B_0$ in $L_2$. The maps $A_k \to B_k$ join to $f\colon A_\omega \to B_\omega$, and the maps $B_k \to A_{k+1}$ join to $g$ with $gf = \mathrm{id}$ and $fg = \mathrm{id}$. So $f$ is an $L$-isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Transport the $L_2$-structure of $B_\omega$ onto $A_\omega$ along the isomorphism.
steps.detail: Give the universe of $A_\omega$ the $L_1$-structure of $A_\omega$ and the remaining $L_2$-symbols through $f$. The $L$-symbols agree because $f$ is an $L$-isomorphism. The structure satisfies $T_1$, since $A_\omega \models T_1$, and $T_2$, since $B_\omega \models T_2$. So $T_1 \cup T_2$ has a model and is consistent.

concepts.c:consistent-theory: A consistent theory has a model, and a theory with a model is consistent.
concepts.c:first-order-theory: The two theories are the sets of sentences that the chains must satisfy.
concepts.c:elementary-equivalence: Elementarily equivalent reducts are what allow each amalgamation step.
concepts.c:diagram-of-a-first-order-structure: The diagram lists the facts about elements that the extension must keep.
concepts.c:elementary-embedding: The embeddings preserve all $L$-formulas, which makes the union an isomorphism.

source.note: Robinson's amalgamation proof by alternating elementary chains, as in Chang and Keisler, Model Theory, chapter 2.

statement: Let $G$ be a [finite group](c:finite-group) and $I$ the [augmentation ideal](c:augmentation-ideal) of its [Burnside ring](c:burnside-ring) $A(G)$. Then the map from $G$-[equivariant stable cohomotopy](c:equivariant-stable-cohomotopy) of a point to the stable cohomotopy of the [classifying space](c:classifying-space) $BG$ induces an isomorphism $\pi^n_G(S^0)^\wedge_I \cong \pi^n_s(BG_+)$ in every degree $n$. In degree $0$ this reads $A(G)^\wedge_I \cong \pi^0_s(BG_+)$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group).
The ideal $I$ is the [augmentation ideal](c:augmentation-ideal) of the Burnside ring $A(G) = \pi^0_G(S^0)$, the kernel of the map $A(G) \to \mathbb{Z}$ that counts points.

conclusion: The map $\pi^n_G(S^0) \to \pi^n_s(BG_+)$ is completion at $I$: it induces an isomorphism $\pi^n_G(S^0)^\wedge_I \cong \pi^n_s(BG_+)$ for every integer $n$.

proofs.name: Reduction to elementary abelian groups
proofs.slogan: Reformulate the claim as completion of the equivariant sphere, reduce to $p$-groups, settle elementary abelian groups by Ext computations, and induct to all $p$-groups.
proofs.scope: The proof is an outline that rests on the cited work. It treats the statement for a point; the version for finite $G$-complexes is another member of the family.

roles.why: Finiteness of $G$ lets the Burnside ring split by idempotents and reduces the claim to $p$-subgroups.
The ideal $I$ gives the topology in which the completion is taken.

steps.slogan: Restate the claim as completion of the equivariant sphere spectrum along the map to its Borel completion.
steps.detail: Let $S$ be the $G$-equivariant sphere spectrum and $F(EG_+, S)$ its Borel completion. On $G$-fixed points the map $S \to F(EG_+, S)$ is $\pi^*_G(S^0) \to \pi^*_s(BG_+)$. The theorem says that this map is completion at $I$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the claim to $p$-groups and $p$-adic completion.
steps.detail: May and McClure show that the statement for all finite groups follows from the statement for [$p$-groups](c:p-group) with $p$-adic coefficients. They use the idempotents of the Burnside ring to localize at each prime.

steps.slogan: Settle the elementary abelian $p$-groups by an algebraic computation.
steps.detail: Lin (for $\mathbb{Z}/2$), Gunawardena (for $\mathbb{Z}/p$) and Adams, Gunawardena and Miller (for all elementary abelian $p$-groups) compute the needed Ext groups over the [Steenrod algebra](c:steenrod-algebra) with the Singer construction. This proves the non-equivariant form for these groups.

steps.slogan: Extend from the elementary abelian groups to all $p$-groups by induction on the order.
steps.detail: Carlsson proves the statement for a $p$-group $G$ assuming it for the proper subgroups and for the elementary abelian case. He analyzes the geometric fixed points through the poset of elementary abelian subgroups, using Quillen's results on such posets.

steps.slogan: Assemble the cases into the completion statement for every finite group.
steps.detail: The reduction to $p$-groups and the $p$-group case give the $p$-adic statement for every prime. This is the statement for $G$ with $A(G)$ completed at $I$. Passing from the map of spectra to homotopy groups gives every degree $n$.

concepts.c:burnside-ring: The Burnside ring is the degree-$0$ equivariant cohomotopy that is completed.
concepts.c:equivariant-stable-cohomotopy: This is the source of the completion map in every degree.
concepts.c:classifying-space: The stable cohomotopy of $BG$ is the target of the completion.
concepts.c:finite-group: Finiteness reduces the claim to $p$-groups and their subgroups.
concepts.c:augmentation-ideal: The completion is taken in the $I$-adic topology.
concepts.c:p-group: The proof reduces the statement to groups of prime power order.
concepts.c:steenrod-algebra: The Ext groups over this algebra give the elementary abelian case.

source.ref: G. Carlsson, Equivariant stable homotopy and Segal's Burnside ring conjecture, Annals of Mathematics 120 (1984), 189-224
source.note: The inputs are J. P. May and J. E. McClure, A reduction of the Segal conjecture (1982), and J. F. Adams, J. H. Gunawardena and H. Miller, The Segal conjecture for elementary abelian p-groups, Topology 24 (1985).

statement: Let $P$ be a [polynomial](c:polynomial) with constant coefficients, $D = d/dx$, and $a$ a constant. For every function $y$ that is differentiable $\deg P$ times, the [linear differential operator](c:linear-differential-operator) $P(D)$ satisfies $P(D)\big(e^{ax} y\big) = e^{ax}\, P(D + a)\, y$, where $e^{ax}$ is the [exponential function](c:exponential-function).

hypotheses.text: The operator is $P(D)$ for a [polynomial](c:polynomial) $P$ with constant coefficients and degree $m$.
The function $y$ is differentiable $m$ times and $a$ is a constant.

conclusion: $P(D)\big(e^{ax} y\big) = e^{ax}\, P(D + a)\, y$ as functions of $x$.

proofs.name: Product rule and induction
proofs.slogan: Move the exponential through one derivative by the product rule, iterate to powers of $D$, then sum over the monomials of $P$.
proofs.scope: Real or complex $a$ and $y$ with $m = \deg P$ derivatives. The identity holds on the whole domain of $y$.

roles.why: The monomials of $P$ reduce the claim to powers of $D$, and constant coefficients commute with $e^{ax}$.
Differentiability to order $m$ makes every derivative $D^k y$ with $k \le m$ exist, so each step is defined.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the product $e^{ax} y$ once.
steps.detail: The product rule for the [derivative](c:derivative) and $D e^{ax} = a e^{ax}$ give $D(e^{ax} y) = a e^{ax} y + e^{ax} D y = e^{ax}(D + a)\, y$.

steps.slogan: Show by induction that $D^k(e^{ax} y) = e^{ax}(D + a)^k y$.
steps.detail: The case $k = 0$ is trivial. If the formula holds for $k$, then $D^{k+1}(e^{ax} y) = D\big(e^{ax}(D + a)^k y\big) = e^{ax}(D + a)(D + a)^k y$, by step 1 applied to the function $(D + a)^k y$.

steps.slogan: Extend to the polynomial $P$ by linearity.
steps.detail: Write $P(t) = \sum_k c_k t^k$. Then $P(D)(e^{ax} y) = \sum_k c_k D^k(e^{ax} y) = e^{ax} \sum_k c_k (D + a)^k y = e^{ax} P(D + a)\, y$.

concepts.c:polynomial: The operator is a polynomial in $D$, which reduces the claim to monomials.
concepts.c:linear-differential-operator: Linearity of the operator lets the identity pass from monomials to $P(D)$.
concepts.c:exponential-function: The exponential is the factor that passes through each derivative.
concepts.c:derivative: The product rule for the derivative moves the exponential past one $D$.

source.note: The classical operator calculus for linear ODEs with constant coefficients; the proof is the product rule and induction.
